countries.posture: Argentina keeps strong satellite engineering through INVAP but faces deep budget cuts, and under Milei its policy is tilting toward the US.

agency.note: Created by presidential decree on May 3, 2010 as an open joint stock company. countries.hsfNote: No national human spaceflight program or provider talks were found, and Azerbaijan's human spaceflight link runs through Türkiye, whose Galactic 07 astronaut carried the Azerbaijani flag in 2024.

countries.industry: Azercosmos is a commercial satellite operator selling capacity and imagery across Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. milestones.text: Azercosmos organized Azerbaijan's first National Space Hackathon.
Azercosmos signed an MOU with Kuwait Space Company.
Azercosmos joined the Digital Intermediate Frequency Interoperability (DIFI) Consortium.

Azercosmos held cooperation talks with Uzbekcosmos at IAC Antalya on October 8.

countries.posture: Azerbaijan pairs a commercial operator model built on Western industry with political alignment with Türkiye through the Organization of Turkic States and with China through ILRS membership since October 2023, and it had not signed the Artemis Accords as of the latest list checked (July 2026).

milestones.text: Economy minister Márton Nagy announced plans for a national space agency and a space law at the REMTECH center.
Tibor Kapu launched to the ISS on Ax-4, the first Hungarian national mission since 1980.

The government said it was preparing a broad agreement with Voyager Technologies on its planned commercial station.

Kapu was named to lead HUNOR until it closes at the end of 2026, and a national agency and space law are under study for 2027.

countries.posture: Hungary is rebuilding its space governance under a new ministry after a 2025 national flight, backed by a more than doubled ESA commitment, Artemis membership and a possible national agency and space law from 2027.

milestones.text: The new Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development took over the space portfolio, with Zhaslan Madiyev as minister.
Entrepreneur Danna Karagussova flew on Blue Origin NS-36 on October 8, becoming the first Kazakh woman in space.
The all-female SANA-1 ten day isolation experiment concluded on October 10 to support future cosmonaut training.
The Soyuz MS-28 launch on November 27 damaged Baikonur's only crewed launch pad, which Roscosmos repaired by March 3, 2026.
The government announced five to six new Earth observation satellites, with about $75 million in planned exports.
Soyuz-5 (Sunkar) made a successful first flight from the Kazakh-Russian Baiterek complex at Baikonur on April 30.
The government allocated 10.4 billion tenge ($22.3 million) for initial development of the KazSat-3R communications satellite.
Kazakhstan joined Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye in the first Organization of Turkic States space cooperation agreement on October 6.

countries.posture: Kazakhstan runs a multi-vector space policy that stays structurally tied to Russia through Baikonur and Baiterek, joined China's ILRS lunar project in July 2024, builds satellites with Airbus and courts foreign investors, and it had not signed the Artemis Accords as of the latest list checked (July 2026).

space.note: No official space budget was found. The February 2026 presidential review of the satellite and cosmonaut projects gave no cost figures. In March 2026 Uzbekcosmos said finding funding sources was still a priority. In mid 2025 Uzbekcosmos estimated that building and launching its own satellite could cost $50 to $100 million.

agency.name: Space Research and Technology Agency Uzbekcosmos
agency.parent: Ministry of Digital Technologies (Minister Sherzod Shermatov)
agency.note: Created by presidential decree on August 30, 2019. Kadirov was in post as director by September 2024, when he was elected chair of the CIS Interstate Space Council, and led the agency at IAC Antalya in October 2026. His start date was not found. Deputy Director Mukhiddin Ibragimov is the main public voice on the cosmonaut project.

countries.hsfNote: Uzbekcosmos targets a 10 to 14 day orbital flight for its first national cosmonaut by October 2028 to coincide with IAC 2028 in Samarkand, and says it is negotiating with the United States, Russia and China, but no provider contract, named candidate or government decision had been made public as of October 21, 2026.

sats.note: No fully national satellite is in orbit. Samarkand-2028, a Chinese-built STAR.VISION hyperspectral Earth observation satellite carrying an onboard AI module developed by Uzbekcosmos engineers, launched on August 5, 2026 from a sea platform off Shandong. Uzbek official sources describe it as a partner mission rather than a national satellite. The first national scientific satellite, the 6U CubeSat Mirzo Ulugbek, is being built by Uzbek engineers at Kyushu Institute of Technology for a 2028 launch. A joint Organization of Turkic States scientific satellite is planned for 2027.

countries.industry: Uzbekistan inherited Soviet aerospace assets, including the Tashkent aircraft plant and a design bureau that built the Luna 24 soil sampler, but most of that capacity closed by the mid 2000s. Current activity centers on Uzbekcosmos remote sensing services used by more than ten state agencies, engineer training abroad, and partner projects with China's STAR.VISION, Vast and Hungary's 4iG.

milestones.text: Samarkand was selected to host the 79th International Astronautical Congress, set for October 9 to 13, 2028.
The Ministry of Digital Technologies signed an MOU with Vast to involve Uzbek specialists in human spaceflight, including possible Haven-1 missions.
President Mirziyoyev reviewed plans for the 6U Mirzo Ulugbek satellite in 2028 and a 10 to 14 day flight for the first national cosmonaut.
Uzbekcosmos announced an open nationwide cosmonaut selection and a government commission with two working groups.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov offered to prepare and fly Uzbekistan's first cosmonaut and launch its first satellite.

orgs.name: Swedish Institute of Space Physics (IRF)
orgs.desc: Kiruna government research institute building space plasma and particle instruments flown on ESA and international missions (BepiColombo, JUICE, Mars/Venus Express). One of Europe's most experienced instrument houses.

orgs.name: Swedish National Space Agency (SNSA)
orgs.desc: Government agency under the Ministry of Education and Research responsible for national space activities, ESA contributions and space research funding. Co-sponsored Sweden's participation in an ESA project astronaut flight and manages national programs in EO, microgravity research and launch infrastructure.

orgs.name: Unibap Space Solutions
orgs.desc: Uppsala company behind SpaceCloud, radiation-tolerant AI/edge-computing hardware and software for in-orbit data processing, flown on multiple missions. One of Europe's most established orbital edge-computing players.

orgs.name: Abdi İbrahim
orgs.desc: Türkiye's largest pharmaceutical company (Istanbul) with major GMP manufacturing, biotech investments (AbdiBio) and international operations across 50+ markets.

orgs.name: ASELSAN
orgs.desc: Türkiye's largest defense-electronics company, avionics, communications, EO/IR systems and space-qualified electronics (TWTAs, transceivers for Türksat and Göktürk), investing in microelectronics and chip capability.

orgs.name: Baykar
orgs.desc: Türkiye's leading UAV manufacturer (Bayraktar TB2, Akıncı, Kızılelma) with large-scale advanced manufacturing, avionics and AI/autonomy capability, leadership founded Fergani Space, extending the group into orbital systems.

orgs.name: DeltaV Space Technologies
orgs.desc: Ankara propulsion company developing hybrid rocket engines, including the engine for Türkiye's planned Moon mission, and sounding rockets tested to space altitudes.

orgs.name: Fergani Space
orgs.desc: Baykar-affiliated space company that launched Türkiye's first private satellites (FGN-100 series, from Jan 2025) toward a planned LEO positioning/PNT constellation of 100 satellites, with in-house production in Istanbul.

orgs.name: HAVELSAN
orgs.desc: Turkish defense-software major (2,600+ staff): C4ISR, simulation and training centers (F-16, A320/B737), cyber security and national-scale ICT.

orgs.name: Istanbul Technical University (ITU)
orgs.desc: Historic Turkish engineering university with an aeronautics/astronautics faculty, cubesat heritage (ITUpSAT1, Türkiye's first university satellite) and an active space-systems design lab ecosystem.

orgs.name: Middle East Technical University (METU / ODTÜ)
orgs.desc: Türkiye's top engineering research university (Ankara) with aerospace engineering, the METU-Teknokent technology park hosting space companies, and deep ties to TÜBİTAK and national space programs.

orgs.name: Plan-S
orgs.desc: Turkish satellite and space-data company building the Connecta IoT and EO smallsat constellations, with multiple satellites launched since 2022 and its own production and ground-segment operations.

orgs.name: Roketsan
orgs.desc: Turkish propulsion and missile company developing the national Micro Satellite Launch System (MUFS), sounding rockets that reached space altitude, and hybrid/liquid propulsion, a pillar of independent access to space.

orgs.name: SAHA Istanbul
orgs.desc: Türkiye's largest defense, aviation and space industry cluster with 1,000+ member companies, supplier development, certification and internationalization programs (SAHA EXPO, SAHA Academy).

orgs.name: TÜBİTAK BİLGEM (YİTAL semiconductor line)
orgs.desc: TÜBİTAK's informatics and security research center hosting YİTAL, Türkiye's national IC design and fabrication capability, cooperating with industry (incl. ASELSAN) on homegrown chip production amid a national semiconductor push.

orgs.name: TÜBİTAK Space Technologies Research Institute (UZAY)
orgs.desc: Türkiye's principal space research institute (Ankara), builder of national EO satellites (RASAT, Göktürk-2, İMECE) and coordinator of the Ax-3 science program (13 Turkish experiments) and the suborbital research flight.

orgs.name: Turkcell (Google Cloud region)
orgs.desc: Lead Turkish telco building the country's first hyperscale data-center region with Google Cloud ($2B Google + $1B Turkcell, announced Nov 2025), Türkiye targets ~$10B to become a regional AI/DC hub by 2030.

orgs.name: Turkish Aerospace (TUSAŞ / TAI)
orgs.desc: Türkiye's largest aerospace company, aircraft, UAVs and the national satellite integrator (Türksat 6A, Göktürk) with a large Space Systems AIT center in Ankara and thousands of engineers.

orgs.name: Turkish Space Agency (TUA)
orgs.desc: National space agency (2018), owner of the National Space Program including the human-spaceflight program that flew Alper Gezeravcı to the ISS on Ax-3 (Jan 2024) and Tuva Atasever's Axiom-managed suborbital flight. Led by President Yusuf Kıraç, host of IAC 2026 in Antalya.

orgs.name: Türksat
orgs.desc: State-owned satellite operator running the Türksat GEO fleet (incl. domestically built Türksat 6A) and national teleport/ground infrastructure, plus cable and e-government services.

orgs.name: USET, National Satellite AIT Center
orgs.desc: Ankara-based national satellite Assembly, Integration and Test complex (one of the region's largest AIT facilities), used for Türksat 6A and Göktürk and available for third-party environmental testing.

orgs.name: Yongatek Microelectronics
orgs.desc: Turkish fabless chip designer moving homegrown MCUs to mass production in 2026 (30M+ annual units with Beko), 12nm AI camera chips planned via TSMC 2027 to 28, 5G NTN chip in development.

orgs.name: Artel Electronics
orgs.desc: Central Asia's largest home-appliance and consumer-electronics manufacturer (Tashkent), with large-scale electronics assembly, PCB-level manufacturing experience and regional export operations.

orgs.name: Beeline Uzbekistan (VEON)
orgs.desc: Uzbekistan's largest telecom operator, anchor tenant of DataVolt's TAS-1 data center and a driver of sovereign data/cloud services.

orgs.name: Center for Space Monitoring & Geoinformation Technologies
orgs.desc: State center under the national space agency for satellite data reception, processing and geoinformation services for government users (agriculture, cadastre, emergency monitoring).

orgs.name: DataVolt (TAS-1)
orgs.desc: Saudi-backed developer building Uzbekistan's flagship AI data center (TAS-1, Tashkent IT Park) with a Bukhara expansion under exploration, Beeline anchored as tenant (Jun 2026).

orgs.name: IT Park Uzbekistan
orgs.desc: State technopark and residency regime for IT companies with tax incentives and 1,500+ residents, central instrument of Uzbekistan's IT export and AI/ICT ecosystem growth.

orgs.name: Jurabek Laboratories
orgs.desc: One of Uzbekistan's largest pharmaceutical manufacturers (Tashkent), producing generics across a wide range of dosage forms with GMP-oriented production and regional exports.

orgs.name: Ministry of Digital Technologies
orgs.desc: Ministry led by Sherzod Shermatov driving digital transformation, sovereign cloud strategy, data-center buildout (incl. a Karakalpakstan data-center hub) and IT sector growth, oversees IT Park Uzbekistan.

orgs.name: National University of Uzbekistan
orgs.desc: The country's oldest and largest classical university (Tashkent), strong in physics, chemistry and biology, aligned with the research themes announced for the first astronaut mission.

orgs.name: Tashkent University of Information Technologies (TUIT)
orgs.desc: Uzbekistan's leading ICT university (al-Khwarizmi) with regional branches and active links to Uzbekcosmos youth and satellite-engineering initiatives (engineers trained in Japan on satellite building).

orgs.name: Ulugh Beg Astronomical Institute
orgs.desc: Historic Academy of Sciences astronomy institute operating the Maidanak Observatory, one of Eurasia's best optical astronomy sites, with international collaboration on space-object observation and astrophysics.

orgs.name: Uzbekcosmos (UZCOSMOS)
orgs.desc: National space agency under the Cabinet of Ministers, national space program, remote sensing and international cooperation. orgs.name: Uzpharmagency
orgs.desc: Government agency under the Ministry of Health developing Uzbekistan's pharmaceutical industry, drug-production localization, pharma FDI attraction and free economic zones for pharma manufacturing.

United Launch Alliance builds rockets in Decatur, and Blue Origin builds rocket engines in Huntsville.

NI.profile: Lower Saxony is research-led in space, with DLR sites in Braunschweig, Göttingen, Hanover and Trauen. Hanover hosts the DLR Institute for Satellite Geodesy and Inertial Sensing and the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics, while Göttingen hosts the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research and DLR spacecraft aerodynamics testing, and TU Braunschweig runs an Institute of Space Systems. At Trauen near Faßberg, DLR's Responsive Space Cluster Competence Center (RSC3) develops technology for rapid satellite and launch capability with federal defense funding. The state backs the sector through its Niedersachsen Aviation initiative, which hosted the 20th German Aerospace Regions Day in Hanover on 22 September 2026.

NW.office: Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Industrie, Klimaschutz und Energie des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen (Ministry of Economic Affairs, Industry, Climate Action and Energy)
NW.profile: North Rhine-Westphalia hosts the DLR headquarters and the ESA European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, with the LUNA lunar analog facility and the :envihab space medicine facility on the same campus, and the German Space Agency at DLR in Bonn. The Bundeswehr Space Command and the German Space Situational Awareness Centre are based in Uedem, and research capacity includes Fraunhofer FHR with its TIRA radar in Wachtberg and RWTH Aachen. In 2025 the state appointed former ESA astronaut Reinhold Ewald as its first space ambassador, signed memoranda with Axiom Space and Starlab Space, and in November 2025 signed a letter of intent with ESA and DLR to relocate the ESA Directorate of Human and Robotic Exploration to Cologne. In 2026 the state committed 50 million euros to a GOVSATCOM hub in Cologne and Rheinmetall ICEYE Space Solutions started SAR satellite production in Neuss.

RP.name: Rhineland-Palatinate
RP.profile: Rhineland-Palatinate has little civil space industry but hosts major military space functions. Ramstein Air Base is home to the NATO Space Centre at Allied Air Command (AIRCOM, established 2020) and to U.S. Space Forces Europe and Africa (activated 2023), and the Bundeswehr procurement office BAAINBw in Koblenz contracts German military satellite programs. Civil activity is limited to niche suppliers and research, including SCHOTT in Mainz (ZERODUR glass ceramic and space solar cell cover glass), satellite remote sensing at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry and AI for Earth observation at DFKI Kaiserslautern. The Land has no dedicated space office or strategy.

SN.name: Saxony
SN.office: Luft- und Raumfahrtkoordinator im Freistaat Sachsen (Aerospace Coordinator of the Free State of Saxony), appointed in July 2022, office at TU Dresden
SN.profile: Saxony's aerospace sector counts about 160 companies and research institutions with more than 7,000 employees and about 1.4 billion euros in annual revenue, and is mostly aviation focused. Space activity centers on TU Dresden's Institute of Aerospace Engineering and Dresden firms such as Morpheus Space, which opened a satellite electric propulsion factory in 2024, and NEOSAT, whose acquisition by Rohde & Schwarz was announced in September 2026. In 2025 OHB took over the former TechniSat electronics plant in Schöneck in the Vogtland for series production of space electronics. In 2026 the state economics ministry announced a Space Saxony ecosystem initiative, and a consortium of Saxon companies is planning the SAXON-1 demonstration satellite, targeted for launch in 2027.

TH.office: Thüringer Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Landwirtschaft und Ländlichen Raum (Thuringian Ministry for Economy, Agriculture and Rural Areas), with LEG Thüringen
TH.profile: Space activity in Thuringia is concentrated in Jena's optics and photonics cluster. Jena-Optronik, an Airbus Defence and Space subsidiary, builds star trackers and rendezvous and docking sensors flown on the Artemis program and on the Japanese MMX mission launched in October 2026, alongside Fraunhofer IOF space optics, the DLR Institute of Data Science and Friedrich Schiller University. The state economy ministry counts about 100 aerospace companies and institutions and roughly 11,000 dependent jobs, and in October 2026 it held the first Thuringian Aerospace Day in Jena with LEG Thüringen and the LRT Saxony/Thuringia cluster. There is no dedicated state space strategy.

government.notes: Space policy is decided at presidential level by decree and executed by GGPEN under MINTTICS, with an interministerial commission coordinating ministries. Funding comes from the state budget approved by the National Assembly, historically combined with export credit and intergovernmental financing for satellites from Russia and France. The government announced in October 2025 that GGPEN will be converted into an Angolan Space Agency, but formal creation was not confirmed in this run. President Lourenço is in his final term, and the next general election is expected in 2027.

strategy.summary: Angola's National Space Strategy 2016-2025 was approved by Presidential Decree No. 85/17 and is implemented by GGPEN, the national space program management office under the telecommunications ministry. It is built on five axes: space infrastructure, training and promotion, industry and technology, international positioning, and organization and cooperation. Its horizon has passed and no successor strategy was found, though the government cited it in October 2025 when announcing the conversion of GGPEN into an Angolan Space Agency.

strategy.title: Plan Espacial Nacional 2016-2027 (preliminary version); successor roadmap: Bases para el Desarrollo Espacial Argentino (10 Dec 2025)
strategy.status: preliminary (approved by the CONAE Directorio and presented to the executive; no adopted successor found)
strategy.owner: CONAE (proposes and executes the plan); Directorio of CONAE; presented to the national executive; the Bases were presented by the SICyT
strategy.summary: The official CONAE page describes the Plan Espacial Nacional as a strategic plan, a state policy of national priority, with three components: Earth observation, peaceful exploration and use of outer space, and technological development for space use. The preliminary version 2016-2027 was approved by the CONAE Directorio and presented to the national executive (CONAE page, 2026). On 10 Dec 2025 the SICyT presented the Bases para el Desarrollo Espacial Argentino as a roadmap for a new plan, including a national space hub, a space-access project and an astronaut-training platform, and international value-chain integration. The full bases document was not found on the official site.
strategy.budget: No consolidated budget for the plan is published in the sources opened. Decree of Necessity and Urgency 867/2026, published in the Boletín Oficial on Friday 4 Sep 2026 (regional press, La Capital), increased CONAE resources for programmes and activities linked to space policy; the press report gives no amount. A press-reported real-terms cut of about 65 percent since December 2023 was not verified and is not used.
goals: Earth observation for Argentina's continental and maritime territory (CONAE plan axis)
Peaceful exploration and use of outer space, including cooperative missions (CONAE plan axis)
Technological development for space use and domestic industry (CONAE plan axis)
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space activities law was found. Ley 27208 (Ley de Desarrollo de la Industria Satelital; sanctioned 4 Nov 2015; Boletín Oficial 11 Nov 2015) declares the development of the satellite industry a matter of national interest and state policy (art. 1) and approves the Plan Satelital Geoestacionario Argentino 2015-2035 (art. 2). A 'Ley Espacial Argentina' bill appeared only in a search snippet; its PDF was not readable and it is not used.

strategy.title: Government Programme 2026–2031 (space objective); no standalone national space strategy found
strategy.owner: Government of the Republic of Armenia; authorised state body under Law HO-152-N (not named)
strategy.summary: No standalone national space strategy document was found. The Prime Minister said on 10 Sep 2026 that the Government Programme 2026–2031 makes national space capabilities a standalone strategic objective. The stated goals are at least three national satellites (two Earth observation, one telecommunications), sovereign ground infrastructure, a distributed ground-station network and participation in international programmes. The legal basis is Law HO-152-N on Space Activity (6 Mar 2020), which sets Government approval of development and financing programmes and a Government-authorised state body. A science-sector programme 2026–2030 names space as a priority (PM release; not fetched).
strategy.budget: No space budget line or consolidated national space budget found in the fetched sources. The law finances space activity from the state budget (Art. 9). Budget figures in the seed (AMD 10 million licensing duty; tax incentives to 2030) are not re-proved and are excluded.
goals: Operate at least three national satellites: two Earth observation, one telecommunications (PM release, 10 Sep 2026)
Build sovereign ground-based infrastructure and domestic capacity for satellite command, control, data reception and processing (PM release, 10 Sep 2026)
Establish a distributed network of ground stations for national and international missions (PM release, 10 Sep 2026)
Enable Armenian engineers and companies to contribute to international space programmes (PM release, 10 Sep 2026)
strategy.law: Law of the Republic of Armenia on Space Activity, No. HO-152-N, adopted 6 Mar 2020 by the National Assembly, published 1 Apr 2020 (ARLIS), in force 11 Apr 2020 (ARLIS header and UNEP LEAP). Government decrees on licensing (No. 1984-N), registration and alienation of space objects are listed in UN document A/AC.105/C.2/2025/CRP.6; their texts were not read in this pass.

strategy.title: Space Strategy 2030
strategy.owner: Azercosmos (Space Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan)
strategy.summary: Space Strategy 2030 is published on the Space Agency website as the sector development path to 2030. Its three goals are economic growth and sustainable space development, a national space ecosystem based on research, and national interest through space projects. Priority directions include satellite service sustainability with replacement satellites, local production with a Spacecraft Development Center and at least 50 jobs, national security and backup links, and research, human capital, startups and SMEs. The strategy has no stated budget. Its predecessor is the 2009 State Programme on the Establishment and Development of the Space Industry.
strategy.budget: No budget for Space Strategy 2030 found in any fetched official source. Cabinet decision No. 106 (16 Apr 2026) changes a figure in clause 5.1 of the agency charter from 473 605 880 to 567 605 880; currency and purpose are not stated in the extracted text, so it is not recorded as a strategy budget. The seed USD 120 million satellite purchase (2023 press) is not re-proved.
goals: Ensuring economic growth and sustainable development in space
Formation of a national space ecosystem based on scientific research and application of innovative solutions
Protecting national interests by implementing space projects for peace and prosperity
Priority: sustainability of existing satellite services, including replacement of satellites at end of orbital life
Priority: local production potential, a Spacecraft Development Center with at least 50 jobs
Priority: national security use of satellites and backup links for strategic infrastructure
Priority: expansion of space research and human capital; startups and SMEs
strategy.law: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan on Space Activity (Kosmik fəaliyyət haqqında), No. 927-VIQ, signed 24 June 2023; enters into force 60 days after publication (Article 24). strategy.summary: Bulgaria has no adopted national space strategy. In its 2025 statements to UN COPUOS the government said drafting a National Space Strategy and a National Space Program is its top short-term priority, alongside domestic space legislation and the creation of a national space agency. A draft update to the Innovation Strategy for Smart Specialisation 2021-2027 adds a national priority on space and dual-use technologies (public consultation closed 20 September 2026).

strategy.summary: Cameroon launched a CAMSPACE national space programme in July 2019 (MINPOSTEL inauguration, reported by Space in Africa). The study was awarded to a EUROCONSULT/INTEGC/Digiglobe group under a gré-à-gré authorisation of 14 Sept 2023 (Digital Business Africa, 20 Nov 2024). The Space Security Portal records that Cameroon announced CAMSPACE in October 2023. No national space strategy, national space policy document, space agency or space law was found in primary sources.
strategy.budget: The reported study contract is 2 012 061 089 F.CFA (about 2.01 billion FCFA) per Digital Business Africa, 20 Nov 2024. This is a study contract value, not a programme budget; no programme budget line was found.

strategy.summary: Colombia's most recent adopted space policy is CONPES 3983 of January 2020, which set enabling conditions for the space sector to support national productivity and competitiveness, with an action plan that closed in December 2021. It called for reforming the Colombian Space Commission, reducing barriers for private entry, filing orbit and spectrum resources with the ITU, and commercializing defense satellite capabilities. As of 2025 the Colombian Space Commission reported to UN COPUOS that it was drafting a new National Space Policy to define national space governance and institutions, and no successor policy had been identified as adopted by this date.

strategy.summary: Approved by the government in October 2025, the plan sets the long-term vision for Czechia as an active and internationally recognized space actor that uses space technologies for the economy, society and security. It defines seven strategic goals and seven competence platforms, from satellites up to 500 kg and scientific instruments to Earth observation data processing and space security and defense. It also frames the national Czech Path to Space project, including a Czech astronaut mission to the ISS expected around 2027 to 2028. Coordination of space activities moved from the Ministry of Transport to the Ministry of Industry and Trade on 1 March 2026.

strategy.summary: Germany's national space strategy was adopted by the federal cabinet on 27 September 2023, replacing the 2010 strategy, and treats space infrastructure as critical infrastructure for Germany and Europe. It sets nine fields of action ranging from European and international cooperation and New Space growth to security, sustainability, research and exploration. Since 2025 federal civil space policy has been consolidated in the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR), which told the Bundestag in November 2025 that a decision on rewriting the strategy will follow once its new space department is fully established. A separate Space Security Strategy was presented in cabinet in November 2025.

government.notes: Space decisions in Egypt are concentrated at the presidential level, with the President appointing EgSA's CEO (one-year renewable terms) and board by decree. The Prime Minister chairs the EgSA board, which brings in the higher education, communications and other ministries. Funding comes through the state budget passed by the House of Representatives, while major satellite projects have relied on foreign partner financing and technology transfer agreements. The current CEO, Majed Ismail, was appointed by Presidential Decree No. 439 of 2025.

strategy.summary: Egypt's space policy rests on a 10-year National Space Program prepared by the Egyptian Space Agency and approved in 2020, structured in short, medium and long-term phases running to about 2030. It is aligned with Egypt's Sustainable Development Strategy (Vision 2030) and the decree establishing EgSA. The program emphasizes localizing satellite technology, building national industry and positioning Egypt as a regional and African space hub, including hosting the African Space Agency at Egyptian Space City.

strategy.summary: Spain has no single adopted national space strategy. Its civil space policy rests on the Spanish Space Agency (AEE), created by Royal Decree 158/2023 under the joint authority of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities and the Ministry of Defense, and on the 2022 Aerospace PERTE investment plan. On the security side, the 2019 National Aerospace Security Strategy, adopted under the National Security Council, still frames policy. In 2023 the science minister set a Space Law and a National Space Plan as AEE objectives, and the government has committed 455 million euros a year to ESA through 2030.

strategy.summary: Published on 8 September 2026, the UK Space Strategy replaces the 2021 National Space Strategy and brings civil, defense and security space into one plan, with a delivery plan to 2029/30 and longer term goals to 2035. Its two top level outcomes are defense and national security, and growth of the UK economy, supported by sector wide foundations on industrialization, partnerships, pro growth regulation and resilience. A technical delivery annex sets out funding lines for financial years 2026/27 to 2029/30.

strategy.title: Ghana Space Policy
strategy.horizon: No end year stated. The policy's implementation matrix sets timelines from 1 year to 5 years.
strategy.owner: Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation (MESTI); implementation by GSSTI and GAEC
strategy.summary: The policy sets a national framework for space science and technology (SST): establishing a Ghana Space Agency, space education, infrastructure, research, applications and commercialisation, international collaboration, a legal and regulatory framework, and outreach. It was approved by Cabinet in March 2022 and unveiled in November 2024. It states the policy 'will be coordinated by' MESTI.
strategy.budget: No appropriated amount found. Policy target: 'Allocate at least 0.1% of GDP for SST activities', with annual budget support for the national space agency and an SST development fund (policy Section 5, Financing; Ministry of Finance named as the responsible body in the implementation matrix).
goals: Establish the Ghana Space Agency as a national entity with legal authority
Space education and human resource development
Build space infrastructure, including ground stations and research centres
Promote space science research and development
Space application and commercialisation of space products
Collaboration with relevant local and international organisations
Legal and regulatory framework, including ratification of the five UN outer space treaties
Space science outreach, education and awareness in schools and to the public
strategy.law: No space act enacted found. The policy (section 4.1.7) commits Ghana to put space laws and regulatory systems in place and to ratify the five UN outer space treaties. Legislation for the Ghana Space Agency is being drafted after Cabinet approval (GNA, 3 Oct 2026; Graphic Online, press conference 5 Oct 2026); no parliamentary stage found. Constitutional authority: Article 58(1) vests executive authority in the President.

other_docs.note: Announced by the Minister on 2 Oct 2026 (GSSTI news; GNA 3 Oct 2026). Graphic Online reports the press conference of 5 Oct 2026. Dates differ across outlets; the approval itself is consistent.

strategy.summary: Greece presented its first National Space Strategy, running to 2030, together with the HELLAS-SPACE 2.0 program at the Greece in Orbit event on 26 June 2026. The strategy follows the first phase national microsatellite program funded through the Recovery and Resilience Facility and ESA, and shifts emphasis from participation in European programs to domestic production and technological autonomy. It sets five national goals and includes a governance system with annual progress reviews. HELLAS-SPACE 2.0 targets national production lines and international tenders with at least 50 percent Greek participation.

strategy.summary: Hungary adopted its first national space strategy in 2021, aiming to use the space sector as a driver of innovation and growth, to strengthen the country's international role, and to build the knowledge base and infrastructure for the sector. Its flagship projects were national satellite and ground segment capabilities and the HUNOR astronaut program, which flew a Hungarian astronaut to the ISS on Axiom Mission 4 in June 2025. After the May 2026 change of government, space coordination moved to the new Ministry of Science and Technology, which has named renewal of the strategy as its first space task, together with closer ESA ties and a new regulatory and institutional framework.

strategy.summary: Indonesia's space policy rests on Law No. 21 of 2013 on Space Activities and the 2017 presidential master plan that sets long term targets to 2040 for space science, remote sensing, space technology, launch and commercial space activities. Since the former space agency LAPAN was merged into the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) in 2021, space research and implementation sit inside BRIN. The master plan is evaluated every five years, and BRIN officials stated in early 2026 that some targets need to be redefined to be more adaptive and realistic. Current priorities are a national spaceport at Biak, Papua, and domestically built Earth observation satellites focused on food security.

government.notes: Strategic direction rests with the Supreme Leader, while the civil program is set by the Supreme Space Council under the President and run by the ICT ministry through ISA and ISRC. Funding comes through the annual budget law approved by the Majlis and through defense channels for the IRGC track, which operates largely outside civil oversight. Mojtaba Khamenei was named Supreme Leader on 8 March 2026 after Ali Khamenei was killed on 28 February, and he has not appeared in verified video or audio since, so his health and role are disputed. The war that began in February 2026 is unresolved as of this date, with a US naval blockade and intermittent strikes, which adds uncertainty to budgets and leadership.

strategy.summary: Iran's space activity is governed by a 10-year roadmap drafted by the ICT ministry and approved by the Supreme Space Council in 2022, which aims to make Iran a regional hub for space technology. Priorities are Earth observation, communications and positioning satellites, sovereign launch capability, and reaching geostationary orbit. The program has continued during the 2026 war despite strikes on facilities, including the Iranian Space Research Center in Tehran. A civil track under the Iranian Space Agency runs in parallel with a military track under the IRGC Aerospace Force.

strategy.summary: Approved at the 29th COMINT meeting on 14 May 2026, the DSPSN is Italy's first comprehensive national planning framework for space and implements the Government Guidelines on Space and Aerospace approved by COMINT in late 2024. It sets priorities for the next decade along four axes: research and benefits for society, industrial competitiveness, governance and regulation, and international cooperation. It treats space as a domain of strategic competition and calls for a national space security strategy, a critical space technologies plan and operational security and defense capabilities. It operates within Law No. 89 of 2025 on the space economy.

strategy.budget: The Space Strategy Fund at JAXA targets about 1 trillion yen over ten years, with 0.8 trillion yen secured as of 2025 (Cabinet Office, 2026). JAXA's annual budget was 215.5 billion yen in fiscal 2023.
goals: Ensure space security, including space domain awareness and resilient satellite systems
Strengthen national resilience and address global issues through Earth observation, positioning and communications
Create new knowledge through space science and exploration, including Artemis lunar participation
Strengthen the industrial and technology base, including H3 launch capability
Double the space industry market from 4.0 trillion yen (2020) to 8.0 trillion yen in the early 2030s
Expand the QZSS regional navigation constellation to seven and later eleven satellites
strategy.horizon: 10 year plan with a 20 year outlook, roadmap revised annually
strategy.law: The Basic Space Act (2008) is the framework law. The Space Activities Act (2016) licenses launches and satellite control, and the Diet passed an amendment in June 2026 that extends licensing to rocket launches generally, adds pre launch certification of space objects and broadens operator liability, with human spaceflight and reusable vehicles left to later rules. The Remote Sensing Data Act (2016) and the Space Resources Act (2021) are also in force.

strategy.title: Kenya Space Agency Strategic Plan 2023-2027
strategy.status: active (horizon 2027; KSA news of 13 May 2024 launch; plan published by KSA)
strategy.owner: Kenya Space Agency (reports to the Board, then to the Cabinet Secretary for Defence)
strategy.summary: The KSA Strategic Plan 2023-2027, copyright 2023 and launched 13 May 2024, sets six key result areas: coordination and regulation of space activities; national space capability development; utilisation of space services; space research, innovation and development; resource mobilisation; and institutional capacity. The predecessor plan 2020-2025 was launched 20 Oct 2020 (KSA history page). The plan states that the DG/CEO reports to the Board, which reports to the CS for Defence.
strategy.budget: Plan: no budget figure in the plan text. FY 2026/27 Budget Estimates (Parliament of Kenya), Vote R1041 Ministry of Defence, sub-programme 1041000107 Kenya Space Agency: KSh 400,000,000 current grant (estimate); KSh 350,000,000 approved for 2025/26; projections KSh 580,000,000 (2027/28) and KSh 695,000,000 (2028/29).
goals: Coordination and regulation of space activities
National space capability development
Utilisation of space services and technologies
Space research, innovation and development
Resource mobilisation
Strengthening institutional capacity
strategy.law: Kenya Space Agency Order, Legal Notice No. 22 of 7 March 2017 (Kenya Law text, revised 31 Dec 2022): establishes the agency under the State Corporations Act; defines the Cabinet Secretary as the one responsible for Defence. A draft Kenya Space Bill 2024 would replace the Order with an Act; not enacted in sources read (April 2024 Government statement: final stage of developing legislation).

government.notes: Kyrgyzstan has no separate space agency found in the sources opened. Space activity is run through presidential decisions and a 2026 Cabinet resolution creating the state company Kyrgyz Sputnik (later Kyrgyz Asman), founded by the Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry. Its first national Earth observation satellite was launched from Vandenberg on 1 October 2026 on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rideshare. The Chairman of the Cabinet also heads the Presidential Administration. The 2027 presidential election date and the Constitutional Court finding of February 2026 are seed claims and are not re-proved here. No national space law was located; the legal database was not searched exhaustively.

strategy.summary: The 4th Basic Plan, decided by the National Space Committee on 21 December 2022, covers 2023 to 2027 and frames the goal of becoming a major space economy power by 2045. It is implemented through annual plans by the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), founded in May 2024 under the Ministry of Science and ICT. A July 2026 National Space Committee meeting accelerated lunar lander timelines and set a domestic LEO communications network target for 2035. The next five-year basic plan is due to cover the period from 2028.

strategy.summary: Luxembourg's national space strategy for 2023 to 2027 is set by the Ministry of the Economy and implemented by the Luxembourg Space Agency (LSA). Its central theme is sustainability, organized around economic sustainability, sustainability of activities on Earth and in space, and the responsible use of space resources. It aims to grow and diversify the space sector as part of the national economy, backed by ESA participation, the national LuxIMPULSE program, and dedicated finance instruments. The strategy horizon ends in 2027, so a successor document is due.

government.notes: Mexico has no comprehensive national space activities law in the sources opened. The Ley que crea la Agencia Espacial Mexicana (DOF 30 Jul 2010) created the AEM as a decentralised public body. The DOF programme (4 Jun 2026) states that the 28 Nov 2024 DOF decree reforming the Organic Law of the Federal Public Administration created the ATDT and that the AEM is sectorised to it; the 2010 law's SCT sector reference is superseded on that basis. The Programa Espacial Mexicano 2026-2030 is issued by the ATDT, with the AEM as technical authority. The AEM had no titular or interim head from 24 Jan 2025, as the ATDT itself acknowledged (Expansión, 12 Mar 2026); no 2026 official page names an AEM head. Head of state and head of government: Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, President of Mexico (one office; no separate prime minister). Presidency press listing dated 26 Oct 2026.

strategy.title: Programa Espacial Mexicano 2026-2030
strategy.owner: Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones (ATDT), with the Agencia Espacial Mexicana as technical authority
strategy.summary: Published in the DOF on 4 June 2026 with the ATDT as issuing body, under the Plan Nacional de Desarrollo 2025-2030 and the ATDT sectoral programme. Its legal basis cites CPEUM arts. 26 and 28, the Ley de Planeación and the 28 Nov 2024 DOF decree that created the ATDT. Initial projects: a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities; a constellation of small Earth-observation satellites; a national centre to process satellite imagery; specialist training; and international cooperation, including ITU coordination of orbital positions and spectrum. The AEM is the technical authority, and the programme states that the AEM had not yet produced a current strategic programme in its institutional phase.
strategy.budget: No dedicated budget figure for the 2026-2030 programme is stated in the programme text. Press (Expansión, 8 Jan 2026, citing the 2026 PEF) reports a federal allocation to the AEM of 46,755 millones de pesos, down 33.1% from 69,950 millones in 2025. The unit and the PEF annex are not verified; a separate press report gives a different scale. Treat as press-reported, unit unresolved.
goals: Build a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities
Deploy a constellation of small Earth observation satellites for civil protection, environment, agriculture, security and territorial planning
Create a national centre to process and analyse satellite imagery from national and commercial systems
Train Mexican specialists for the space sector
Link Mexico to the international space sector and strengthen management of orbital positions and spectrum rights at the ITU
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space activities law found in the sources opened. Founding statute: Ley que crea la Agencia Espacial Mexicana (DOF 30 Jul 2010), which creates the AEM as a decentralised public body; its 2010 sector reference (SCT) is superseded by the ATDT sectorisation stated in the 2026 programme. Constitutional basis: CPEUM art. 28 (satellite communication as a priority area under State rectory) and art. 26 (planning).

strategy.title: Strategy for Scientific Research Activity of Montenegro 2024-2028 (Strategija naučnoistraživačke djelatnosti Crne Gore 2024-2028)
strategy.status: in force per the ministry framework page (2026); Government conclusions on the proposal dated 22 Jul 2024; the adoption wording and adopted text to be confirmed (translation doubt on "bez rasprave")
strategy.horizon: 2024-2028; action plan 2024-2025; draft action plan 2026-2027 (Government conclusions 16 Jun 2026)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation (MPNI), named as "Nosilac aktivnosti" throughout the strategy text
strategy.summary: The research strategy sets three strategic goals: improving framework conditions, strengthening human resources and institutional capacity, and strengthening international cooperation. The strategy was published as a PDF dated Podgorica, July 2024; the Government document library holds conclusions on the proposal (22 Jul 2024) and conclusions on a 2026-2027 draft action plan (16 Jun 2026). The ministry's framework page lists the strategy and a 2025 implementation report. No national space strategy was found; the strategy text read contains no space reference.
goals: Strateški cilj 1: Poboljšanje okvirnih uslova za funkcionisanje naučnoistraživačke djelatnosti u Crnoj Gori (improving framework conditions for research)
Strateški cilj 2: Jačanje ljudskih resursa i institucionalnih kapaciteta u oblasti nauke i istraživanja (strengthening human resources and institutional capacity)
Strateški cilj 3: Snaženje međunarodne saradnje u nauci i istraživanjima (strengthening international cooperation in science and research)
strategy.law: Zakon o naučnoistraživačkoj djelatnosti (Law on Scientific Research Activity), Službeni list CG 80/10, 40/11, 57/14, 82/20, as cited in the strategy (2024); also listed on the ministry framework page
other_docs: Draft action plan for implementing the strategy 2026-2027 (Government document, 28 May 2026, proposal); Government conclusions 16 Jun 2026

strategy.title: National Space Science and Technology Policy (2021)
strategy.status: in force (implementation period 2021/22 to 2029/30; reaffirmed by government, Mar 2026)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sport, Arts and Culture (implementation lead); NCRST (coordinating agency). Issued in 2021 by MHETI.
strategy.summary: Namibia's Cabinet adopted the policy on 23 March 2021 (Cabinet no. 4TH/23.03.21/006), launched 4 June 2021. It has four objectives: awareness; collaboration and funding; human and institutional capacity; access and use of space technology. Cabinet approved drafting a Space Science and Technology Bill in 2025 (press). A national steering committee ran public consultations in 2026 (NBC). No enacted law or space agency was found; the government reaffirmed the policy in March 2026.
strategy.budget: The policy's implementation plan (appendix) has a budget column in N$ thousands per activity; the totals were not extracted. No separate national space budget line was found in the sources opened. The 2026/27 education budget (press) includes N$25.5m for a satellite data ground receiving station at the Windhoek Telecom earth station, a separate site; not confirmed as space budget in an official document. NUST station: government-funded (SIA, Mar 2026), amount not stated.
goals: Improve awareness and appreciation of space science and technology in Namibia (Objective 1)
Ensure collaboration and mobilisation of resources for funding space science and technology (Objective 2)
Build human and institutional capacity in space science and technology (Objective 3)
Ensure optimal access to and use of space technologies (Objective 4)
strategy.law: No space law enacted in sources opened. Space Science and Technology Bill: Cabinet approved drafting (Aug 2025, press); National Steering Committee consultations in 2026 (NBC). Not tabled in Parliament as far as found. Legal basis of NCRST: Research, Science and Technology Act, 2004 (Act 23 of 2004), as cited in the 2021 policy.

strategy.summary: Nigeria's National Space Policy was approved in 2000, and a 25-year implementation roadmap was endorsed in 2005, phased from government-funded development toward commercialization and public-private partnership. Several targets slipped, including a first Nigerian astronaut (originally 2015, later restated for 2030) and a full launch capability. At its first meeting in March 2026, the National Space Council set up an expert working group to revise the 25-year roadmap, with the implementation cost to go to the Federal Executive Council.

ESA subscriptions are split by budget line, with Economic Affairs funding Basic Activities and most optional programs, Education funding Science, and Defence adding conditional one-off contributions counted toward the NATO spending norm. strategy.summary: The Long-Term Space Agenda, prepared on the advice of the Netherlands Space Office and endorsed by the cabinet in February 2025, replaced the earlier three-year policy cycle tied to ESA ministerial conferences. It sets six missions spanning security, climate, science, satellite data, industry and international law. A 2017 to 2024 policy evaluation found the missions insufficiently concrete, and in January 2026 the cabinet committed to prioritize them. The Netherlands Space Office was renamed the Netherlands Space Agency in March 2026 with a stronger mandate.

government.notes: Space policy and regulation sit in one portfolio, with the Minister for Space acting as both policy lead and statutory licensing decision-maker, advised by MBIE and the New Zealand Space Agency (led by an acting General Manager, Space, Andrew Johnson, per the August 2026 briefing). Funding is small and largely flows through MBIE appropriations, Cabinet reprioritizations and the Catalyst Fund rather than a dedicated space budget. Security agencies screen license applications and the 2025 amendment added national security powers over ground stations. The portfolio changed hands twice in 2026 (Chris Penk from 7 April, Paul Goldsmith from 13 August), and a general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 with official results due 27 November 2026, so the incumbent Luxon government continues until a new government is formed.

strategy.summary: Oman's National Space Policy and Executive Program is a ten year framework for 2023 to 2033 that aims to make Oman a regional hub for space applications. It rests on four pillars (economic diversification, national security, capacity building and environmental stewardship) and prioritizes the downstream sector as the entry point. strategy.summary: Pakistan's first National Space Policy was approved by the federal cabinet in December 2023 and sets the country's first legal and regulatory framework for space activities. It frames space as a tool for socioeconomic development and national security, commits to peaceful use, and opens the market to public-private partnerships and foreign low Earth orbit communications providers. SUPARCO implements, monitors and revises the policy, and the Pakistan Space Activities Regulatory Board licenses operators under rules issued in 2024. The policy sits beside the longer running Space Program 2040, which drives a fast satellite launch cadence built mainly with Chinese partners.

strategy.summary: Peru has no adopted national space policy. In July 2024 the Ministry of Defense formally launched the formulation of a Política Nacional Espacial, with CONIDA leading the process and technical advice from the ministry's General Directorate of Policy and Strategy, and in November 2025 CONIDA was still contracting analysis to support the drafting. strategy.summary: The Philippine Space Act, approved on 8 August 2019, embeds the Philippine Space Development and Utilization Policy and created the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) as the central body for space policy and programs. The policy aims to make the country space-capable and space-faring within a decade, organized around six key development areas. Implementation runs through PhilSA, whose Director General holds Cabinet rank and serves as Presidential Adviser on Space Matters, with the Earth observation satellite MULA as the current flagship mission expected to launch in late 2026.

strategy.summary: Portugal Space 2030 was approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 February 2018 together with the draft Space Law, and set the national strategy for space to 2030. It aims to grow a space economy built on data, services and infrastructure, using the Atlantic position of the Azores for launch, return and ground station activities. In 2025 the government set up a Space Interministerial Working Group that shaped a record ESA subscription, and the 2026 agenda centers on the Santa Maria spaceport, reentry operations and the Atlantic Constellation with Spain. No formal successor strategy had been published as of this file.

strategy.owner: No adopted strategy owner found. The national model is set out as SSC oversight, SSA implementation and CST regulatory support (UN COPUOS 2025 statement).
strategy.summary: No adopted national space strategy document was located in the official sources opened on 27 Oct 2026. The 2025 UN statement describes the institutional model, not a strategy. A government report, "Digital and Space Sustainability 2026", issued by CST in August 2026, projects the sector rising from USD 8.7 billion in 2024 to USD 31.6 billion by 2035; it is a market projection, not a strategy or budget. The report itself was not opened (reported by Okaz, 29 Aug 2026).
strategy.budget: No public space budget line was located in the sources opened. The USD 8.7bn (2024) to USD 31.6bn (2035) figure is a sector projection in a CST report as reported by Okaz; it is not an appropriation.
goals: Develop and localize space science and technology (SSA objective)

Provide applications and practices in satellites and exploratory missions (SSA objective)
Enhance the Kingdom position as a leading regional and international centre in space (SSA objective)
Adopt expertise in applied space research for civil purposes (SSA objective)
strategy.law: No space statute in force. Draft Space Sector Regulations and Guidelines were put to public consultation via the Istitlaa platform (Umm Al-Qura, 5 Jan 2026; closing 24 Mar 2026). CST told COPUOS in June 2026 that a draft Space Law and executive regulations are in preparation. Bill number and stage not confirmed.

government.notes: Space decisions in Singapore are made by the Cabinet and executed through NSAS, a department of the trade and industry ministry, which coordinates civil, industrial and international space activity and is drafting space legislation. Defense space work runs through MINDEF, DSTA and DSO, and the NSAS Chief Executive came from DSO and DSTA. The trade and industry ministry was renamed the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry from 1 October 2026 following the July 2026 cabinet changes. Funding flows through ministry budgets approved by Parliament.

strategy.summary: Singapore has not published a national space strategy document. The policy basis is the mandate of the National Space Agency of Singapore (NSAS), established on 1 April 2026 under the trade and industry ministry, which took over the Office for Space Technology and Industry (OSTIn) and has five pillars: national space capabilities, R&D, industry, international partnerships and space legislation. Operational guidance comes from the 2024 Guidelines for Singapore Related Space Activities, and funding from the S$210 million Space Technology Development Program set aside since 2022. Official statements say Singapore does not prioritize launch capability because of land constraints.

government.notes: Serbia has no space agency, so space decisions run through the Government and individual ministries, with the Ministry of Science as the de facto lead and funder through its research budget. International commitments are driven by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Artemis Accords, 2026) and sector bodies (RHMZ for EUMETSAT, BioSense for Copernicus). The political setting is in flux: President Vucic resigned on 27 September 2026 to run for Prime Minister, Speaker Ana Brnabic is acting President, the National Assembly is dissolved ahead of the 25 October 2026 snap election, and a presidential election must follow within three months. Prime Minister Djuro Macut (in office since 16 April 2025) leads the government until a new one is formed.

government.notes: The Riksdag sets space appropriations in the annual budget, with civil space funds channeled through the Ministry of Education and Research to the Swedish National Space Agency and military space funds through the Ministry of Defence. Recent space decisions have been issued jointly by the Education, Defence and Finance ministries. Kristersson asked to be released after the left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority in the September 2026 election and leads a caretaker government. On 15 October 2026 the Riksdag rejected Magdalena Andersson as prime minister by 248 votes to 99, and government formation was still ongoing as of 23 October 2026.

strategy.budget: ESA CM25 subscription of EUR 305 million, 1.36 percent of the ESA total, of which EUR 138 million to optional programs. The agency's 2027 to 2029 budget request proposes SEK 2.08 billion for appropriation 3:4 Space research and space activities in 2027, rising to about SEK 2.95 billion in 2029. The 2026 spring amending budget added SEK 400 million, with SEK 386 million in equity for SSC launch capability at Esrange and SEK 14 million for licensing at the Swedish National Space Agency. Military space is funded separately through the Armed Forces space billion for 2024 to 2032 and a SEK 1.3 billion military satellite package announced in January 2026.
goals: Promote peaceful and sustainable use of space and help develop international rules, including on space debris
Make space data easily accessible across society, including EU navigation and Earth observation services
Use state space activity to strengthen national security and military capability
Make critical infrastructure resilient to disruption of space services and extreme solar storms
Keep space legislation supportive of domestic activity, international obligations and private investment
Keep participation in ESA and EU programs predictable and strengthen industry competitiveness
Maintain Esrange in Kiruna as a key national and European resource and sustain high quality space research
strategy.law: Act on Space Activities (Lag om rymdverksamhet, SFS 1982:963) remains in force. A new space law is in preparation but no bill had been presented as of this date. In May 2026 the Swedish National Space Agency was tasked with preparing a new licensing organization as a first step.

government.notes: Space policy is set by the National Space Policy Committee, chaired by a Deputy Prime Minister with the digital economy ministry providing the secretariat, and its decisions go to the Cabinet for approval. Implementation and most space funding sit with GISTDA and NARIT under the higher education and science ministry, through the annual budget act passed by parliament. Spectrum and orbital filings are handled by the independent NBTC. Following the 8 February 2026 general election, the House re-elected Anutin Charnvirakul as Prime Minister on 19 March 2026 and the King endorsed his second cabinet on 31 March 2026.

strategy.summary: The Cabinet approved the 15-year National Space Master Plan 2023-2037 in December 2022, alongside a National Communication Satellite Policy. The plan aims to build a space economy that supports national security, prosperity and sustainability through eight strategies covering security, economy and industry, innovation, technology, exploration and international cooperation. In July 2025 the National Space Policy Committee gave initial approval to a revised master plan that incorporates recommendations from the National Economic and Social Development Council and still requires formal approval.

strategy.summary: Taiwan's space policy is set by the Phase III National Space Program, announced in 2019 for 2019 to 2028 with an expected cost of NT$25.1 billion and a target of at least one satellite launch per year. It shifts Taiwan from single satellites to constellations, with domestic optical, SAR and low Earth orbit communications satellites, launch vehicles and a national launch site. The Taiwan Space Agency, an administrative corporation under the National Science and Technology Council, implements the program. TASA describes its two main goals as strengthening national security and promoting the space industry.

The 2022 agency bill (Carpeta 3275/2022) would sit within the Presidency; its status in 2026 is not confirmed. A Nov 2024 decree places the national space-object registry under the Air Force. Head of state and government are the same office under the presidential system (Constitution art. 149).

strategy.summary: Decision 169/QD-TTg, signed by the Prime Minister on 4 February 2021, sets Vietnam's space science and technology strategy through 2030 and builds on the 2006 national space technology strategy. It targets a mid-level position in space science and technology in Southeast Asia by 2030, mastery of small high-resolution Earth observation satellite technology, replacement of the VINASAT communication satellites and a large expansion of the space workforce. At the March 2026 inauguration of the Vietnam National Space Center, the government restated these targets and said it is moving toward a national space law.

Local government elections are set for 4 November 2026, and national government is a multiparty Government of National Unity.

iaf.about: The International Astronautical Federation is a non-governmental space advocacy organization founded in 1951 and headquartered in Paris, France. Its members include space agencies, companies, universities, research institutes and professional societies from around the world. It organizes the annual International Astronautical Congress together with topic-specific global conferences, ministerial and parliamentary meetings, awards and programs for students and young professionals.

conferences.name: Small Satellite Conference
conferences.organizer: Utah State University and its Space Dynamics Laboratory, with AIAA
conferences.about: Annual technical conference on small satellite missions, technology and business, started by two Utah State University professors in 1987 and held in Logan for nearly four decades before moving to the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City in 2025 because Logan lacked the hotel capacity. It attracts engineers, researchers, students, agencies and companies, with an estimated 3,700 to 3,800 attendees from nearly 40 countries in 2024.

conferences.name: United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space
conferences.organizer: United Nations, with the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) as secretariat
conferences.cadence: Annual, main session in June, Scientific and Technical Subcommittee in February, Legal Subcommittee in April
conferences.about: The Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space is the United Nations committee for international cooperation in the peaceful exploration and use of outer space, made permanent by the General Assembly in 1959 and serviced by UNOOSA. Member State delegations and accredited observer organizations meet at the Vienna International Centre for the main Committee session in June and for its Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and Legal Subcommittee sessions earlier in the year.
